mainText: Good morning. Here is your curated AI briefing for Saturday, September 26, 2026. The most notable development today involves the intersection of AI, privacy, and personal digital twins. Synthesia, a startup valued at $4 billion, has debuted an interactive AI avatar of a journalist, demonstrating a new capability for its platform. While digital avatars have previously been used to read scripts in training videos, this interactive model—built using voice-to-text, agentic language models, and text-to-voice technology—can listen to and answer questions. The avatar was trained on a specific report written by the journalist, highlighting how enterprises might soon use these tools for roleplay, sales training, or internal knowledge sharing. This matters because it signals a shift toward more conversational, autonomous AI agents in professional settings, though it also raises questions about the normalization of digital likenesses in the public sphere. In other news, Meta is doubling down on its commitment to smart glasses. At the company's annual Connect event, Meta highlighted several new wearable devices, including audio-only glasses designed to assist the hearing impaired. Priced at $150, these devices aim to provide a more affordable alternative to traditional hearing aids, which can cost significantly more, while integrating with Meta’s personal AI agent, Muse. While the company intends for these glasses to help users manage digital tasks like email and scheduling, early demonstrations showed potential friction, as the AI agent occasionally struggled to distinguish between the wearer's commands and casual conversation. This development underscores Meta's strategy to move beyond screen-based computing, though it also faces ongoing public and regulatory scrutiny regarding surveillance and privacy, particularly given recent accusations that camera-equipped versions could be used for illicit recording. Additionally, the Department of Defense is seeking $30.3 million to develop Polygraph Next, a program aimed at updating lie-detection technologies. The proposal focuses on using AI and machine learning to analyze physiological responses through non-contact, standoff sensors, such as cameras capable of tracking facial temperature, pulse, and pore activity. While the government says the project aims to modernize credibility assessment for security vetting and insider threat detection, the initiative faces skepticism from legal scholars and historical data. Past reports from the National Research Council have cited limited evidence for the efficacy of polygraphs, and critics warn that deploying an imperfect system across the department’s 2.8 million employees could lead to widespread false accusations. On the infrastructure front, Amazon Web Services has released new architectures to improve the efficiency of training large language models. The company detailed how using Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service alongside specialized networking adapters like the Elastic Fabric Adapter and the DeepEP library can help address the complexities of Mixture-of-Experts model training. These tools are particularly important during reinforcement learning phases, where they help balance the competing demands of rollout generation and policy training, potentially increasing throughput by 40 percent. Separately, researchers at the firm Netskope reported a rise in sophisticated tech support scams delivered through Google Ads. These malicious ads target both Windows and Mac users by freezing browsers and displaying fake security alerts to trick individuals into calling fraudulent support centers. While Netskope noted that its security tools prevented its clients from falling for these specific campaigns, the firm warned that the true scale of the impact is likely much larger than observed, as many users remain vulnerable due to a lack of technical awareness. In the business sector, OpenAI highlighted how one of its clients, the fleet management software provider Proaction, has integrated the AI tool Codex into its sales operations. By using the model to analyze customer data and build customized product demos, the firm reports that it has significantly reduced the time engineering teams spend on sales support, saving between 40 and 60 engineering hours per month.
